## Part 2: Evolving stars

### (T11.2a)

During the main sequence, the central helium mass fraction increases steadily up to $Y_{c,\max}=1-Z_c$. Here the maximum is reached at age around 8.5 Gyr from the plot of $Y_c$ vs age.

$$\boxed{t_{\mathrm{MS}}=8.5\times10^9\ \mathrm{yr}}.\qquad[1.0]$$

| Half credit lower limit | Full credit range | Half credit upper limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | $8.0\times10^9$ yr to $9.0\times10^9$ yr |  |

### (T11.2b)

During He-burning the central $Y$ decreases steadily to zero. The inset of $Y_c$ shows ages $11.896\times10^9$ to $11.960\times10^9$ yr, corresponding to 64 Myr.

$$\boxed{\Delta t_{\mathrm{He}}=64\times10^6\ \mathrm{yr}}.\qquad[1.0]$$

| Half credit lower limit | Full credit range | Half credit upper limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | $62\times10^6$ yr to $66\times10^6$ yr |  |

### (T11.2c)

Read the $\log L$ vs age graph to get age $\approx4\times10^9$ yr. [1.0]

At this age $Y_c\approx0.60$, so $X_c\approx1-0.60-0.02=0.38$. [1.0]

The fraction of original H burnt is
$$\boxed{f_H=1-\frac{X_c}{X_0}=1-\frac{X_c}{1-Y_0-Z_0}=0.46}.\qquad[1.0]$$

| Half credit lower limit | Full credit range | Half credit upper limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.39 | 0.45 to 0.46 | 0.53 |

Expression in % or fraction is ok.

### (T11.2d)

$$X_0=1-Y_0-Z_0=1-0.28-0.02=0.70.$$
When 60% of H has burnt, $X_c=0.40X_0=0.28$.
$$Y_c=1-X_c-Z_c=1-0.28-0.02=0.70.\qquad[2.0]$$

From the $Y_c$ graph, the age is $\sim5\times10^9$ yr. From the graph of $\log R$, the radius is $\sim1\,R_\odot$ ($\log(R/R_\odot)\approx0$).

$$\boxed{R_1=1\,R_\odot}.\qquad[1.0]$$

Any other answer is unlikely since it would involve eye approximation of reading of graphs, that is not to be credited.

### (T11.2e)

For P: $\log T_{\mathrm{eff}}=3.74$, so $T_{\mathrm{eff}}\sim5500$ K ($L$ being flat does not help here). [1.0]

The $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ graph gives age $\sim11\times10^9$ yr, then $\log R\sim0.25$, so
$$\boxed{R_P=1.78\,R_\odot}.\qquad[1.0]$$

| Half credit lower limit | Full credit range | Half credit upper limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | $1.78\,R_\odot$ to $1.80\,R_\odot$ |  |

Only credit of 0.5 in final step if left as $\log R/R_\odot=0.25$.

For Q: $\log L=2.5$ (One can also use $\log T_{\mathrm{eff}}=3.60\implies T_{\mathrm{eff}}\approx3981$ K which would require rounding off to 3950 K at the next step). [1.0]

The inset of $\log L$ gives age $\approx11.884\times10^9$ yr. This value occurs twice; take the first, ascending RGB. $\log R\sim1.6$, so
$$\boxed{R_Q=39.81\,R_\odot}.\qquad[1.0]$$

| Half credit lower limit | Full credit range | Half credit upper limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  | $39.8\,R_\odot$ to $40.0\,R_\odot$ |  |

Only credit of 0.5 in final step if left as $\log R/R_\odot=1.6$. Answer should be same if using $T_{\mathrm{eff}}$ in the first step.

## Part 3: Mass distribution inside a star

### (T11.3a)

$$\frac{dq}{dx}=\frac{dq}{dm}\frac{dm}{dr}\frac{dr}{dx}\qquad[0.5]$$
$$=\frac1M\left[4\pi(Rx)^2\rho\right]R
=3\left(\frac{4\pi R^3}{3M}\right)x^2\rho
=3\left(\frac1{\bar\rho}\right)x^2\rho.\qquad[1.0]$$
$$\boxed{\frac{dq}{dx}=3x^2\sigma}.\qquad[0.5]$$

### (T11.3b)

Let us denote the line as $\log\sigma=\alpha\log x+\beta$.

From the graph, use two endpoints $(-0.5,1.0)$ and $(-0.1,-1.0)$. Therefore,
$$1.0=-0.5\alpha+\beta,\qquad -1.0=-0.1\alpha+\beta.$$
Solving, we get $\alpha=-5$ and $\beta=-1.5$. Therefore,
$$\log\sigma=-5\log x-1.5\quad\text{for }-0.5<\log x<-0.1.\qquad[2.0]$$
$$\sigma(x)=10^{-1.5}x^{-5}\quad\text{for }0.32<x<0.80.$$
$$\boxed{\sigma(x)=0.030x^{-5}}\quad\text{for }0.32<x<0.80.\qquad[2.0]$$
Not rounding off $10^{-1.5}$ is acceptable with full credit.

### (T11.3c)

$$\frac{dq}{dx}=3x^2\sigma=3x^2(0.030x^{-5})=0.090x^{-3}.\qquad[1.0]$$
Integrating, we get
$$q(x)=\int0.090x^{-3}\,dx\qquad[1.0]$$
$$=-\frac{0.045}{x^2}+C\quad(C\text{ is a constant of integration}).\qquad[1.0]$$
Without the constant of integration, only 0.5 marks is given in the last step. Now, given that $q(x=0.35)=0.7$. Using this, we get $C=1.067$. [2.0]

Therefore (rounding off to within 0.005),
$$\boxed{q(x)=1.065-\frac{0.045}{x^2}}\quad\text{for }0.32<x<0.80.\qquad[1.0]$$
If consistent with rounding off at earlier steps, values between 1.065 and 1.091 for the constant term are acceptable with full credit.

### (T11.3d)

$$\frac{dq}{dx}=3x^2\sigma=3x^2(Ax+B)=3Ax^3+3Bx^2.\qquad[1.0]$$
Integrating, we get
$$q(x)=\int(3Ax^3+3Bx^2)\,dx\qquad[1.0]$$
$$=\frac{3A}{4}x^4+Bx^3+D\quad(D\text{ is a constant of integration}).\qquad[1.0]$$
Without the constant of integration, only 0.5 marks is given in the last step.

Three boundary conditions applied sequentially to find the constants:

- Mass at the centre is zero, i.e., $q(0)=0\implies D=0$. [0.5]
- $\rho(0)=80\bar\rho$ (given), i.e., $\sigma(0)=80\implies\boxed{B=80}$. [1.5]
- Given $q(0.25)=0.50$. Therefore,
$$0.5=\frac{3A}{4}(0.25)^4+80$$
$$\implies A=\frac43\frac{0.50-80(0.25)^3}{(0.25)^4}$$
$$\implies\boxed{A=-256}.\qquad[2.0]$$

Therefore, putting the values of $A$ and $B$,
$$\boxed{q(x)=-192x^4+80x^3}\quad\text{for }0\le x\le0.32.\qquad[1.0]$$
Using continuity at $x=0.32$ instead of either of the above conditions will not be credited, since discontinuity has been indicated in the question.

### (T11.3e)

| Slope is zero at both ends | 1.0 |
| Curve passes through the two given points | 1.0 |
| Initial part of the curve looks like a cubic-quartic | 0.5 |
| Latter part of the curve looks negative inverse-square with a dc shift | 0.5 |
| Curve is overall smooth | 0.5 |

problems.title: Hawking Radiation from Black Holes

sections.title: (T12.1) Stellar mass blackholes
sections.statement: A black hole (BH) typically forms by the gravitational collapse of a massive star at the end of its life cycle to a point called a singularity. Due to the extreme gravity of such an object, nothing that enters the so-called event horizon (a spherical surface with $r=R_\mathrm{SC}$, where $r$ is the distance from the singularity) is able to escape from it. Here, $R_\mathrm{SC}$ is referred to as the Schwarzschild radius.

parts.label: (T12.1a)
parts.statement: **Modelling the origin of Hawking radiation:** Consider a pair of particles, each with mass $m$, produced on either side of the BH horizon. One particle is slightly outside the horizon at $r\approx R_\mathrm{SC}$, while the other particle is inside the horizon at $r=\kappa R_\mathrm{SC}$. Assume that the total energy of a particle is the sum of its rest mass energy $mc^2$ and the gravitational potential energy due to the BH. Determine the value of $\kappa$ for which the particle pair has zero total energy.

parts.label: (T12.1b)
parts.statement:
**Temperature of a black hole:** If the particle produced outside the horizon in the above process has enough kinetic energy, it may escape the BH in a process called Hawking radiation. The one inside the horizon, which has negative energy, gets absorbed and decreases the mass of the BH.

Assume that all Hawking radiation is made of photons with a black body spectrum which peaks at the wavelength $\lambda_\mathrm{bb}\approx16R_\mathrm{SC}$. It is known that for a solar mass BH, $R_{\mathrm{SC},\odot}=2.952\,\mathrm{km}$.

Obtain an expression for the temperature, $T_\mathrm{bh}$, of the BH corresponding to this black body radiation, in terms of its mass $M_\mathrm{bh}$ and physical constants. Calculate the Schwarzschild radius, $R_{\mathrm{SC},10\odot}$, and temperature, $T_{\mathrm{bh},10\odot}$, for a BH with mass $10M_\odot$.

parts.label: (T12.1c)
parts.statement:
**Mass loss of a black hole:** Assume that the Hawking radiation is emitted out from the event horizon. Using the mass-energy equivalence, obtain an expression for the rate of mass loss, $dM_\mathrm{bh}(t)/dt$, in terms of the mass $M_\mathrm{bh}(t)$ of the BH and physical constants.

Hence, obtain an expression for $M_\mathrm{bh}(t)$ for a BH with initial mass $M_0$. Sketch $M_\mathrm{bh}(t)$ as a function of $t$ from $M_\mathrm{bh}=M_0$ to $M_\mathrm{bh}=0$.

parts.label: (T12.1d)
parts.statement: **Lifetime of a black hole:** Obtain an expression for the lifetime $\tau_\mathrm{bh}$ at which a black hole with initial mass $M_0$ completely evaporates due to Hawking radiation, in terms of $M_0$ and physical constants. Calculate the lifetime $\tau_{\mathrm{bh},10\odot}$ (in seconds) for a black hole with $M_0=10M_\odot$.

parts.label: (T12.1e)
parts.statement:
**Black hole in a CMB radiation bath:** Consider an isolated black hole in space, far away from other bodies, with a current temperature $T_\mathrm{bh}^\mathrm{now}$, surrounded by the cosmic microwave background (CMB) with a current temperature $T_\mathrm{cmb}^\mathrm{now}=2.7\,\mathrm{K}$. The black hole can grow in mass by absorbing CMB radiation, and lose its mass by Hawking radiation.

Taking into account the accelerating expansion of the Universe, identify which of the following figures show the long-term time evolution of $T_\mathrm{bh}$ in the following three cases:

(X) $T_\mathrm{bh}^\mathrm{now}>T_\mathrm{cmb}^\mathrm{now}$, (Y) $T_\mathrm{bh}^\mathrm{now}=T_\mathrm{cmb}^\mathrm{now}$, (Z) $T_\mathrm{bh}^\mathrm{now}<T_\mathrm{cmb}^\mathrm{now}$.

![All six original black-hole temperature options I–VI with complete curves and native time/temperature labels.](q12-temperature-options)

Indicate your answer by ticking the appropriate box (only one) for each case X, Y or Z in the Table given in the Summary Answersheet corresponding to the appropriate figure number.

sections.title: (T12.2) Primordial black holes
sections.statement: Primordial black holes (PBHs) of much smaller masses can form in the very early Universe. All the following questions are related to PBHs. Here, any processes that increase the mass of the black hole may be neglected.

parts.label: (T12.2a)
parts.statement:
**PBH evaporating at the current epoch:** As you may have noticed from the answers to the previous questions, black holes of solar mass would take a long time to evaporate. However, since PBHs can have a much smaller mass, we may be able to see them evaporating in current times.

Find the initial mass $M_{0,\mathrm{PBH}}$ (in kg), Schwarzschild radius $R_{\mathrm{SC},\mathrm{PBH}}$ (in m), and temperature $T_\mathrm{PBH}$ (in K) of a black hole that may be evaporating away completely at the present epoch, i.e., those with lifetime $\tau_\mathrm{PBH}=14$ billion years.

parts.label: (T12.2b)
parts.statement:
**Formation of a PBH:** In the radiation-dominated early Universe, the scale factor varies as $a(t)\sim t^{1/2}$. In this era, PBHs form due to the collapse of all energy contained in a region of physical size $ct$, where $t$ is the age of the Universe at that time.

A PBH with mass of $10^{12}\,\mathrm{kg}$ forms when the age of the Universe is about $10^{-23}\,\mathrm{s}$. Calculate the age of the Universe, $t_{20}$, when a PBH of mass $10^{20}\,\mathrm{kg}$ forms.

parts.label: (T12.2c)
parts.statement:
**Observed spectrum of Hawking radiation from PBH:** Consider a PBH of initial mass $10^{10}\,\mathrm{kg}$ which completely evaporates at the end of its lifetime $\tau_\mathrm{PBH}$. For this part, assume for simplicity that most of the Hawking radiation is emitted at this time, with a temperature corresponding to its initial mass. Also, take the scale factor of the Universe to be evolving as $a(t)\sim t^{2/3}$.

Calculate the peak wavelength of this Hawking radiation as observed at Earth, $\lambda_\mathrm{earth}$, at the present epoch (at $t=14$ billion years).

parts.label: (T12.2d)
parts.statement:
**High energy cosmic radiation from PBH:** Now assume that the Hawking radiation emitted at a given time $t$ corresponds to photons emitted with an energy $k_BT_\mathrm{bh}(t)$. Also, the highest possible temperature for a black hole is the Planck temperature $T_\mathrm{Planck}$ where $k_BT_\mathrm{Planck}=10^{19}\,\mathrm{GeV}$.

The evolution of the scale factor over relevant time scales is given in the following figure. The scale factor today is set to be unity. $t$(s) on the time axis represents the age of the universe in seconds.

![Complete original scale-factor graph, full logarithmic time/scale axes, ticks, blue curve and orange grid.](q12-scale-factor)

If a photon with an energy of $E_\mathrm{det}=3.0\times10^{20}\,\mathrm{eV}$ is observed on Earth, determine the largest and the smallest possible values of the initial mass of the PBH ($M_0^\mathrm{max}$ and $M_0^\mathrm{min}$, respectively) which could be responsible for this photon.

## Part 1: Stellar mass black holes

### (T12.1a)

- Total energy of any particle is $E=E_{\mathrm{grav}}+mc^2$, so we have

- Then
$$\frac1\kappa=\frac{2c^2R_{\mathrm{SC}}}{GM_{\mathrm{bh}}}-1=3,$$
where we have used $R_{\mathrm{SC}}=2GM_{\mathrm{bh}}/c^2$. [1.0]
- This gives $\boxed{\kappa=\frac13}$. [1.0]

### (T12.2b)

$$M=\frac1{c^2}\rho\left(\frac{4\pi}3\right)\left(\frac{ct}2\right)^3.\qquad[2.0]$$
- With $a(t)\sim t^{1/2}$ and $a(t)\sim1/T$, one gets $t\sim T^{-2}$. [2.0]
- With $\rho\sim T^4\sim t^{-2}$, the mass of PBH formed at time $t$ would be $M_{0,\mathrm{PBH}}\propto t$. [1.0]

### (T12.2d)

- Using the expression for $T_{\mathrm{bh}}$ found in (T12.1b), the energy of a typical photon emitted at time $t$ for a PBH is
$$E_{\mathrm{emitted}}(t)=k_BT_{\mathrm{bh}}(t)=\frac{bc^2k_B}{32GM_{\mathrm{bh}}(t)}.\qquad[1.0]$$
- From (T12.1c), we know
$$M_0^3=3\frac{\pi b^4\sigma c^2}{16^4G^2}t+M_{\mathrm{bh}}(t)^3=3At+\left(\frac{bc^2k_B}{32GE_{\mathrm{emitted}}(t)}\right)^3.\qquad[1.0]$$
- The value of $E_{\mathrm{det}}$ can be different from $E_{\mathrm{emitted}}$ due to redshift. Hence, the smallest possible value of $E_{\mathrm{emitted}}(t)$ is $E_{\mathrm{det}}=3.0\times10^{20}$ eV. This gives the maximum value of the second term as
$$\left(\frac{bc^2k_B}{32GE_{\mathrm{emitted}}(t)}\right)^3_{\max}=4.3\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{kg^3}.\qquad[1.0]$$
- Given the value of $A=3.868\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{kg^3\,s^{-1}}$, the second term can always be neglected for $t\gtrsim10^{-19}$ s. This is true in this problem. So $M_0\approx(3At)^{1/3}$. [1.0]
